summary: At over 7,300 square miles, Riverside County is larger than Connecticut and Rhode Island combined, stretching from the dense subdivisions of the western Inland Empire all the way to the desert floor at Joshua Tree National Park and the Salton Sea — meaning two residents of the same county can live nearly three hours apart and experience entirely different climates, economies, and landscapes. That geographic sprawl is the defining fact of life here: the western third around the cities of Riverside, Corona, and Moreno Valley functions as a massive bedroom community feeding commuters toward Los Angeles and Orange County, while the Coachella Valley to the east runs on tourism, agriculture, and healthcare. With a median home value of $510,300 against a median household income of roughly $89,700, the buy-in sits at about a 5.7-to-1 price-to-income ratio — meaningfully more accessible than coastal Southern California, which is precisely why the population has swelled past 2.5 million. Logistics and warehousing have reshaped vast stretches of the county, with distribution centers lining the I-10 and I-15 corridors alongside UC Riverside and March Air Reserve Base as major employers. Daily highs average 80°F with over ten hours of sunshine year-round, which sounds idyllic until July pushes well past 100°F inland. The essential tension is that the same affordability gap that draws people here also generates the punishing commutes that define their daily lives.
